summary: This RFC explains how to run address translators in networks with very many customers without needing a correspondingly large pool of private IPv4 address space. The approach uses bindings tied to the interface, so the same private addresses can be reused across customers.

eli5.summary: Every classroom can have a Desk 1 and a Desk 2 because the room number says which desk. This lets many customers reuse the same private numbers.

questions: how to scale nat for many customers
how to reuse private ipv4 addresses behind a nat
subtitle: Let one NAT serve any number of customers by keying its mappings to the link each customer arrives on.

tldr.problem: Networks with more than 2^24 (16 million) users cannot give each user a unique private IPv4 address, because the largest private block is 10/8.
tldr.mechanism: A NAT keeps each mapping per internal interface as well as per transport connection, so every point-to-point link can reuse the same private address range.
tldr.outcome: Few IPv4 addresses can serve a huge number of devices, with no tunnels and no changes to the hosts. It only suits point-to-point links, and devices behind the NAT cannot reach each other directly.

today: RFC 6619 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2012, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Running Out of Private Addresses
sections.content:
Networks that serve more than 2^24 (16 million) users cannot assign each a unique private IPv4 address, because the largest reserved private block is 10/8. The RFC says many networks, for instance in the consumer Internet service market, were already hitting that limit, and so could some single devices such as cellular network gateways or mobile IP home agents.

Giving every user a public address would avoid the problem, but the IPv4 pool was becoming depleted. The text notes that the IANA free pool held only 12 unallocated unicast /8 prefixes. Turning some of those into private space would add operational overhead and shrink the public supply. Segmenting a network into areas of overlapping private space severely complicates its design and operation. The move to IPv6 will remove the limit eventually, but during coexistence translation is needed to reach IPv4 destinations.
sections.eli5: There are only so many house numbers in a street. When the street gets enormous, you need a way to reuse numbers without mixing up the houses.

sections.title: The Core Idea
sections.content:
A NAT normally sits between a private IPv4 domain and the public Internet. It holds a public address and keeps a mapping for each session, translating packets so outside traffic uses only public addresses. In a shared-media broadcast network each device needs a unique private address, so it is natural for the NAT to use that address to find the right mapping.

The RFC points out that this is not an inherent requirement. When the NAT connects devices through individual point-to-point links and has another way to identify the mapping, the same private addresses can be used many times, so any number of devices can sit behind a NAT using very few IPv4 addresses.

Tunneling techniques such as the one in RFC 6333 can give the same benefit over any IP network. Where point-to-point links already exist, an extra tunnel layer is unnecessary and could harm MTU settings. This approach can live inside a single device, has no effect on hosts, adds no tunnel endpoint discovery or tunnel security, and leaves packet paths unchanged. Cellular gateways, which already terminate many tunnels, are named as a good fit. PPP, PPPoE, ATM PVCs and per-subscriber VLANs are also listed as relevant links. The address overlap is only at the network edge and does not hurt routing or server reachability.
sections.eli5: If each child has a separate hallway to the teacher, two children can both be called "Sam" and the teacher still knows which hallway Sam came down.

sections.title: Per-Interface Bindings
sections.content:
A NAT using this mode MUST manage its mappings per interface. Each NAT session is tied to the usual five tuples on both sides of the NAT and also to the internal interface that the user device is connected on. That lets every internal interface use the same private IPv4 range. The interface need not be physical; it may be a tunnel, VLAN or other identifiable channel.

If exactly one user device sits on each tunnel and all tunnels give their devices the same IPv4 address, storing that address in the mapping is redundant. When the interface identifier is shorter than 32 bits, this may shrink mapping entries slightly. In other deployments both the device address and the interface identifier probably need storing, which makes entries slightly larger.

This mode is only suitable where devices connect over point-to-point links. If supported, it SHOULD be configurable and should be disabled by default in general-purpose NAT devices. Like all translators it makes devices behind it hard to address, and reusing one address space for different devices means unique private addresses cannot be used to talk between devices behind the same NAT.

The text uses "NAT" to cover both Basic NAT and NAPT, as defined in RFC 2663.
sections.eli5: The NAT writes down which doorway each visitor used, not just their name. Two visitors with the same name are told apart by their doorway.

sections.title: IPv6 Deployment Models
sections.content:
Saving private address space still matters during the move to IPv6, because communication with the IPv4 Internet will be needed for a long time. The RFC recommends two deployment models.

In the first, dual stack, IPv6 uses global addresses and direct end-to-end communication, while IPv4 still needs private addressing and NATs. Per-interface mappings are RECOMMENDED for the IPv4 side. They help the NAT scale, and moving key traffic to IPv6 reduces how much the NAT has to process.

In the second, address and protocol translation such as the stateful NAT64 of RFC 6146 is used and there is no IPv4 in the internal network at all. This only works where all relevant devices and applications are IPv6 capable. Per-interface mappings could be used but are generally unnecessary, since IPv6 addresses are plentiful enough to tell mappings apart.
sections.eli5: If most of the school moves to a new, much bigger numbering system, the old numbering needs far less help. Where both are used, the room trick helps the old one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says these practices do not change the security properties of address translation. From outside, a regular NAT and one using per-interface bindings cannot be told apart.

Point-to-point links mean devices behind the NAT cannot talk to each other directly without passing through the NAT or a router. Because different devices share the same address space, a NAT operation must occur between two devices for them to communicate. For the general security implications of translation, the text refers to RFC 2663, RFC 2993, RFC 4787 and RFC 5382.
sections.eli5: Nobody outside can tell you use the doorway trick. Kids inside also cannot pass notes straight to each other without the teacher in the middle.
